items.title: CADE30008 Flight Dynamics & Advanced Control
items.text:
These pages hold the lecture handouts and slides for the control half of CADE30008 Flight Dynamics & Advanced Control, at the University of Bristol.

They assume you have taken the year 2 unit Dynamics and Control of Linear Systems, or equivalent. You should be comfortable with Laplace transforms, transfer functions, Bode plots and the standard step-response specifications.

Start here

Preparing for Control checks that your laptop, tablet or MATLAB set-up can run the course code — a few minutes, and worth doing early. It also points at the MathWorks Onramp courses and a short diagnostic quiz, both recommended rather than required.

items.title: AI in this course
items.text: This page sets out how I think about generative AI in engineering and in learning; my advice for students; how I use it to make and maintain these materials; and how you can help improve them.

items.title: AI rewards expertise
items.text:
Sean Goedecke makes an argument I agree with: language models reward expertise.1 They let anyone produce seemingly passable work in almost any field, but many outputs fall down against an expert eye, and (importantly in engineering) against the real world.

Goedecke's example is Fields Medal-winning mathematician Terence Tao's conversation with ChatGPT about the Jacobian conjecture, on 20 July 2026.2 Tao's skill is evident, and demonstrates advanced LLM usage, but its utility is highly dependent on human judgement in prompting and evaluating output.

For you, the engineering student, understanding the fundamentals of the discipline is what will make you a good engineer, and a responsible and effective user of whatever tools support you in your work. If you don't, you'll just be wrong faster, and won't know.

Engineering is a real-world discipline and the quality and diligence of our work can have life-or-death impact. Accountability lies with the human-in-the-loop.

items.title: Work or gym?
items.text:
In September 2026, Tao and 24 other Fields Medallists published a joint declaration on the impact of AI on mathematics, the people within it, and the future of the discipline.3 Part of their argument is about how mathematicians are made. Considering this is important in how we support and assess our students.

Bruce Schneier uses an analogy.4 Before using AI on a task, ask whether the task is work or gym.

  • Work is a task where only the outcome matters. Nobody cares how it got done, as long as it's done well, noting that - particularly in engineering - accountability matters.
  • Gym is a task where doing it is the point, because doing it is what builds your ability. Sending a machine to lift your weights moves the weights, but you don't change.

At university, most tasks are gym, even when they look like work. Writing up a design feels like work, but the thinking you do to write it clearly is the gym, and it's what we're trying to assess.

The same task can be either, depending on why you're doing it. Chasing down an obscure Simulink error at eleven at night, when you already understand what your model should do, is (mostly) work. Working out why your loop has less phase margin than you expected is the gym: the struggle is what changes you.

items.title: What that means in this unit
items.text:
• You may use AI, including the AI and agentic tools in MATLAB and Simulink, in the ways the coursework brief lists. The coursework is in the University's Category 3, "Selective".
  • You won't need it. You can do everything in this unit, to the highest standard, without any AI tool.
  • You are responsible for everything you submit, including anything a tool produces. Checking what an AI tool gives you is now an engineering skill.
  • If you can't explain it, you don't understand it yet.

items.title: How these materials were made
items.text:
I use generative AI tools to help create these resources: drafting outlines, writing and checking code, building this site, and keeping all of the pieces consistent with each other.

The pedagogy and the content are mine: what is taught, in what order, how, and why. I have quality-assured and rewritten all of the content.

Teaching, and all formative and summative assessment, are carried out by people. Automated scripts help with technical checks, such as whether your code runs and reproduces your results; those scripts are conventional code, not generative AI, and they don't award marks.

items.title: Why I work this way
items.text:
A course like this is a complex learning journey. My aspirational goal is a series of lectures, with handouts, slide decks, example sheets, code in two languages, figures, and interactives; a coursework that builds through the term; periodic checks; a hands-on laboratory. Every piece has to agree with every other, and has to keep agreeing, every year, as I change things.

That is a great deal of consistency to hold in one head, and it is exactly the kind of tracking a language model is good at — provided it works to robust, explicit, written guidance, and a subject and teaching expert stays in the loop.

I have a suite of 'principles' and 'implementation' docs that I use behind the scenes to try to keep the LLM doing things in the way that I want, but it's often a time-consuming battle.

I use scripts that I've developed with LLM support to check that numbers, figures, slides and handouts agree: every number on a slide traces to the handout, every figure to the code that made it, and every code snippet has been run, in Python and MATLAB, with both giving the same answer. The model tracks; I decide. I use a back-end tool that I and an LLM have developed to keep track of review, approval, and release of materials.

I'm new to this. I'm using this course to develop principles that I want to deploy in other courses, and to share with other educators — as long as it supports my students' learning and experience.

items.title: Where I've gone wrong so far
items.text:
It's easy to begin to allow the LLM to think for you - it can provide suggestions, links to learning theory, draft content, all the way to producing the full unit itself. It's especially easy to start to lean on these tools when things get busy and time is short.

The first few lectures I delivered in this way were in a busy time and I went too far, embarrassed myself, and didn't do my students justice - I'm grateful to those of them who gave constructive feedback that got me back on track.

My strong recommendation is that it's far better to do fewer things well than try to do everything you can possibly dream of but skimp on the QA.

items.title: Tell me what you think
items.text:
I welcome feedback, both specific and general: an error in a derivation, a figure that doesn't make sense, a badly posed question, a broken link — or a view on whether this whole approach works.

  • On GitHub. If you're comfortable doing so, raise an issue in the course's repository. An issue is simply a public note describing a problem; you don't need to know how to use git. Say which page, and what's wrong.
  • By email. You're equally welcome to write to me at steve.bullock@bristol.ac.uk.

items.title: Glossary
items.text:
Looking for a symbol rather than a word? Notation lists every symbol we use, what it means, and the other names you may have met for it.

Every term this course uses, defined once, in plain words. If a lecture and this page disagree, tell us: one of them is wrong.

Definitions here are working ones. They are meant to be enough to follow the argument, not to be the most general statement that could be made. Where a term has a sharper definition you will meet later, that is said.

How to use this page

Use your browser's find (Ctrl+F or Cmd+F), or the site search, which covers this page too. Terms are grouped by where you meet them, not alphabetically, so that reading a whole section makes sense on its own.

items.title: The design process
items.text: Term What it means Control design cycle The loop this course is built on: state the requirements, get a model, design a controller, analyse it, verify it, implement it, then find out what you got wrong and go round again. Every lecture says where in this cycle it sits. Requirement A statement of what the control system must achieve, written so that you can test whether it did. "Settles within 2 seconds with no more than 10 per cent overshoot" is a requirement. "Responds nicely" is not. Specification Used interchangeably with 'requirement' in most control writing. Where this course distinguishes them, a requirement is what the system must do and a specification is the agreed numbers that express it. Plant The thing being controlled: the aircraft, the helicopter rig, the motor. Everything outside the controller. Model A mathematical description of the plant that is good enough for the job in hand. Every model is wrong somewhere; the skill is knowing where. System identification, or system ID Getting a model from measured data rather than from physics. You excite the system, record what it does, and fit a model to the recording. The counterpart to deriving a model from first principles, and often the only honest route when the physics is uncertain. Model-based design The industrial form of the design cycle, in which one set of models carries the work from requirements through simulation and verification to the code that runs on the aircraft. The point is that the model is the shared artifact, not a drawing that gets out of date. Verification Checking that the design meets its requirements. "Did we build it right?" Validation Checking that the model, or the requirements, describe reality. "Did we build the right thing, and does our model of it hold?" Operating point, or trim A condition the aircraft is holding steady at: a speed, an altitude, an attitude, with the forces balanced. Models are usually built around one. Linearisation Replacing the true nonlinear behaviour with a straight-line approximation valid near an operating point. It is what makes almost every tool in this course applicable, and it is the first assumption to question when a design misbehaves far from trim.

items.title: The feedback loop
items.text: Term What it means Open loop The plant driven directly, with no measurement fed back. The Quanser helicopter cannot be flown open loop, which is why the course starts there. Closed loop, or feedback The output is measured, compared with what was wanted, and the difference used to drive the plant. Reference, or setpoint What you want the output to be. Error Reference minus measured output. What the controller acts on. Disturbance Anything that pushes the plant around that is not your control input: gusts, turbulence, a shifting load. Measurement noise Error in the sensor's reading. Feedback acts on it just as readily as on real motion, which is why more gain is not always better. Feedforward Acting on a known reference or a measured disturbance directly, without waiting for an error to appear. Used alongside feedback, not instead of it. Actuator What moves the plant: a control surface and its servo, a motor, a thruster. Saturation An actuator reaching its limit and being unable to give more. The commonest reason a design that worked in simulation fails in reality. Rate limit A limit on how fast an actuator can move, as distinct from how far. It behaves like a delay that gets worse the harder you push. Time delay Any lag between a command and its effect: computation, communication, actuator response. Delay costs phase, and phase is what stability margin is made of.

items.title: PID control
items.text: Term What it means PID Proportional–integral–derivative control: the controller formed by adding three terms computed from the error. By a wide margin the most used controller in engineering, and the first one to try. Proportional term Acts in proportion to the present error. More of it means a faster response and, usually, less stability. Integral term Acts on the accumulated error over time. It removes steady offsets, at the cost of phase and therefore of stability margin. Derivative term Acts on how fast the error is changing, which is a crude prediction of where it is going. It adds damping, and it amplifies measurement noise, so it is almost always used with a filter. Gains The three constants \(K_\mathrm{p}\), \(K_\mathrm{i}\), \(K_\mathrm{d}\) that set how much of each term is used. Tuning means choosing them. Tuning Choosing gains to meet the requirements. It has rules of thumb, it has systematic methods, and it has no single right answer until the requirements are stated. Integral windup The integral term accumulating while the actuator is saturated and nothing can be done about the error. The result is a large, delayed overshoot when the actuator comes off its limit. Preventing it is called anti-windup. Derivative kick The large transient the derivative term produces when the reference is stepped, because the error jumps. Fixed by differentiating the measurement rather than the error. Ziegler–Nichols A classical set of tuning rules from measured characteristics of the plant. Historically important, widely taught, and rarely the best answer.

items.title: Describing behaviour
items.text: Term What it means Transfer function The relationship between a system's input and its output, written in the Laplace variable \(s\). The compact description that most of this course works with. First-order lag A system with one pole and no zero, \(1/(1 + s/\omega_\mathrm{c})\). It passes slow signals through unchanged and attenuates fast ones, falling at 20 dB/decade above its corner. The same object is called a first-order low-pass in signals work. The commonest building block there is: sensors, actuators and filters are mostly lags. Pole A root of a transfer function's denominator. Poles determine how a system responds on its own: how fast it settles, whether it oscillates, whether it diverges. Zero A root of the numerator. Zeros shape how the response starts, and a zero in the right half-plane makes a system initially go the wrong way. Characteristic equation The characteristic polynomial, below, set to zero. Its roots are the closed-loop poles, so it is where stability is decided, and writing it down is usually the first thing you do with a loop. Characteristic polynomial The same denominator, left as a polynomial in \(s\) rather than set to zero. The polynomial is what you write down and factorise; the characteristic equation is the question you ask of it, so the two carry the same information. Reading its coefficients is often faster than finding its roots: if a gain is missing from the coefficient of \(s\), then no amount of that gain changes how fast the response decays, whatever it does to the frequency. Stability A stable system, disturbed, returns to where it was. An unstable one does not. For a linear system this is exactly the question of whether every pole lies in the left half-plane. Marginal stability Poles exactly on the boundary: the system neither settles nor diverges, but oscillates forever. A mathematical case rather than a practical one, since nothing real sits exactly on a boundary. Damping ratio, \(\zeta\) How quickly oscillation dies away, on a scale where 0 oscillates forever and 1 does not oscillate at all. For a simple second-order system it sets the overshoot, about a quarter at \(\zeta = 0.4\) and a twentieth at \(\zeta = 0.7\). Raising it is not free: more damping also means a slower response, so a design chooses between the two rather than hunting for the highest \(\zeta\) it can get. The Quanser helicopter's elevation axis measures near 0.06, which is why it swings for so long after a disturbance. Ringing Informal for a decaying oscillation. You will meet it mostly in electrical and signal work, where a circuit or a trace on a scope rings, and much less for mechanical systems. Control texts say oscillation, and so do we, but the two mean the same thing. Natural frequency, \(\omega_\mathrm{n}\) How fast an oscillatory system wants to move. Together with the damping ratio it fixes a second-order response entirely. Overshoot How far past the target the response goes, as a percentage of the step. For a simple second-order system the damping ratio sets it, and nothing else does; add a third pole or a zero and that stops being true. Rise time, settling time, steady-state error How fast it gets there, how long until it stops moving, and how far off it ends up. With overshoot, the usual language of a time-domain requirement. Step response What the system does when the reference jumps. The most readable single test of a control system, and the one most requirements are written against. Residual What is left when you subtract a model's response from an experimental measurement it is meant to describe. Fit percentage, NRMSE Normalised root mean squared error (NRMSE), a basic indication of how well a model fits against measured data. Range of validity The frequencies or times, the amplitudes, and the operating point over which a model has been shown to describe the machine. DC gain What a system multiplies a constant input by, once everything has settled. Set \(s = 0\) in the transfer function and read off \(G(0)\).

items.title: Frequency domain
items.text:
Term What it means Frequency response How a system responds to sinusoids of each frequency: by how much it magnifies them, and by how much it delays them. A complete description of a linear system, obtained by measurement as readily as by calculation. Bode plot Magnitude and phase of the frequency response, plotted against frequency on logarithmic axes. The working diagram of classical control design. Nyquist plot The frequency response drawn as a path in the complex plane. Harder to read than a Bode plot, and it answers the stability question definitively where the Bode plot can mislead. Nyquist criterion The rule that decides closed-loop stability from the shape of that path, including for plants that are unstable open loop. Loop gain Controller times plant, taken round the loop once. Nearly every classical result is a statement about it. Crossover frequency Where the loop gain passes through 1. Roughly, the fastest the closed loop can be expected to act. Bandwidth The range of frequencies over which the closed loop follows its reference. More bandwidth means a faster system, more actuator effort, and more noise let through: a choice, not a free good. Gain margin How much extra gain the loop can take before it goes unstable. Phase margin How much extra phase lag, or equivalently how much extra delay, the loop can take before it goes unstable.

A margin is not a safety guarantee

A loop can have textbook margins and still be fragile, because margins measure two particular directions of change and a real plant varies in many. Treat them as a necessary check, not a certificate.

Term What it means Sensitivity How much a disturbance, or a change in the plant, reaches the output. Design largely consists of pushing it down where it matters and accepting that it rises elsewhere. Complementary sensitivity How much of the reference, and of the measurement noise, reaches the output. It and the sensitivity add to one at every frequency, which is the most useful constraint in classical design. Loop shaping Designing by deciding what you want the loop gain to look like against frequency, then building a controller that produces it. Lead and lag compensators Simple controllers that add phase where you need it, or gain where you need it, at the cost of the other. The classical alternative to PID, and the route into loop shaping. Root locus A plot of how the closed-loop poles move as a gain is varied. The bridge between the frequency domain and what the response actually looks like.

items.title: Robustness
items.text: Term What it means Uncertainty What you do not know about the plant: parameters you measured imprecisely, dynamics you left out, behaviour that changes with flight condition. Robustness A design's tolerance of that uncertainty. A robust design still meets its requirements when the plant is not quite what the model said. Model error The difference between the plant and the model of it. Bounding it honestly is more useful than pretending it is zero.

items.title: State space and beyond
items.text: Term What it means State The smallest set of numbers that, with the future inputs, determines the system's future entirely. For an aircraft, its velocities, rates and attitude. State-space model The description of a system as a set of first-order differential equations in its state. It handles many inputs and outputs at once, where a transfer function handles one pair. State feedback Driving the plant from all of its states at once, rather than from the output error alone. Observer, or state estimator Something that reconstructs the states you cannot measure from the ones you can, so that state feedback becomes possible. Controllability, observability Whether the inputs can move every state, and whether the outputs reveal every state. If either fails, no amount of design effort will fix it. Pole placement Choosing state feedback gains so that the closed-loop poles land exactly where you want them. Possible, and not always wise. LQR Linear quadratic regulator: state feedback chosen to minimise a weighted sum of state error and control effort. It turns "how aggressive should this be?" into a choice of weights.

items.title: Aircraft
items.text: Term What it means Handling qualities How an aircraft feels and behaves to the pilot flying it, assessed against published standards rather than against opinion. The usual source of a flight control system's requirements. Short period, phugoid The two longitudinal modes of a conventional aircraft: a fast pitching oscillation, and a slow exchange of speed and altitude. Dutch roll, spiral, roll subsidence The three lateral-directional modes: an oscillation coupling yaw and roll, a slow divergence or convergence in bank, and the rapid damping of roll rate. Stability augmentation system, or SAS Feedback added to improve an aircraft's natural behaviour, without the pilot handing over control. Autopilot mode A named behaviour the autopilot can be in, such as holding altitude or tracking a heading, each with its own loop and its own requirements. Control authority How much the control surfaces can actually do. A design that asks for more than exists is not a design. Pilot-induced oscillation, or PIO An oscillation sustained by the pilot's own corrections, usually because delay or a rate limit has put them out of phase with the aircraft. A control problem with a human in the loop.

items.title: Our systems and tools
items.text:
Term What it means Quanser 3-DoF helicopter The laboratory rig: two motors on a beam, free to move in elevation, pitch and travel. Used from week 1 onwards. Elevation, pitch, travel The rig's three axes: how high the beam is, how the rotor head is tilted, and how far round the base it has rotated. MATLAB, Simulink The numerical environment and its block-diagram modelling tool, both licensed to you by the University. Live Script A MATLAB document that mixes text, code and its output. Several of this course's activities are Live Scripts. MATLAB Drive Cloud storage attached to your MATLAB account, used here to give you data and to collect what you produce in a lecture. python-control The Python library that does what MATLAB's Control System Toolbox does. This course gives both, and they agree. Pyodide Python compiled to run in a web browser, which is how the runnable code on this site works without your installing anything.

items.title: Notation
items.text:
Control notation is not standardised. Every textbook makes slightly different choices, and you will have met some of these symbols under other names. This page lists the symbols we use and what else the same thing gets called, so that a different book or a different lecturer does not read as a different subject.

If a symbol here looks unfamiliar, check the last column

It is probably something you already know under another name. Reading across notations is part of becoming fluent, and you will do it constantly once you are reading papers and datasheets.

items.title: How we chose
items.text:
We follow MATLAB. You will spend more hours reading MATLAB's output than reading any book, so when MATLAB names something, we use its name. The controller is C, the plant is G, and a Bode plot's vertical axis is magnitude, in decibels.

Where MATLAB is silent we follow Dorf and Bishop, the recommended textbook for further reading. Where the two disagree we say so below rather than picking silently.

Three house rules:

  • Descriptive subscripts are upright, variable subscripts are italic. In \(K_\mathrm{p}\), the p abbreviates "proportional", so it is upright. In \(x_i\), the \(i\) is an index that ranges over values, so it stays italic. To decide: could the subscript be replaced by a number?
  • A prime means the closed loop. \(\zeta\) and \(\omega_\mathrm{n}\) belong to the plant; \(\zeta'\) and \(\omega_\mathrm{n}'\) are what the loop built around it ends up with. Tuning a controller does not change the machine, so the two need separate names.
  • Every question and worked example defines its symbols, even the obvious ones. It costs a line and removes all doubt.
  • An equation always carries its left-hand side. You will see \(\omega_\mathrm{d} = \omega_\mathrm{n}\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\), not a bare \(\omega_\mathrm{n}\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\) with its name left in the prose.

The \((s)\) often goes missing, and that's normal

Once it is clear that everything is a function of \(s\), almost everyone drops it: \(L = CG\) rather than \(L(s) = C(s)G(s)\), and \(T = L/(1+L)\) rather than the full form. We do it too, especially on slides.

It means the same thing. One place it matters: \(G(0)\) and \(G(j\omega)\) are particular values of \(G(s)\). When an argument is written out explicitly, it is usually there for a reason.

items.title: Signals round the loop
items.text: Symbol Means Also written \(r\), \(R(s)\) Reference, or setpoint — what you're asking for. \(y_\mathrm{d}\), \(\theta_\mathrm{ref}\), "command", "demand". \(y\), \(Y(s)\) Output — what the system actually does. \(C(s)\) in some books, which we avoid: here \(C\) is the controller. \(e\), \(E(s)\) Error, \(e = r - y\) for unity feedback. \(u\), \(U(s)\) Control signal — what the controller asks the actuator for. \(m\) in older texts. \(d\), \(D(s)\) Disturbance — anything that moves the output without being asked. \(T_\mathrm{d}(s)\) in Dorf, which we avoid because \(T_\mathrm{d}\) is also derivative time. \(n\), \(N(s)\) Measurement noise — what the sensor adds that isn't real.

items.title: Blocks
items.text: Symbol Means Also written \(G(s)\) The plant: what you are controlling. \(P(s)\), \(G_\mathrm{p}(s)\). \(C(s)\) The controller: what you design. \(G_\mathrm{c}(s)\) in Dorf, \(K(s)\), \(D(s)\). Note some courses use \(C\) for the output — here it is always the controller. \(H(s)\) The sensor, in the feedback path. Usually 1. \(L(s) = C(s)G(s)\) Loop gain, or open-loop transfer function — what you get going once round the loop. \(G_\mathrm{ol}\), \(GH\). \(T(s)\) Closed-loop transfer function, reference to output. Also called the complementary sensitivity, once sensitivity has been introduced. \(S(s)\) Sensitivity: reference to error, \(S(s) = 1/(1 + L(s))\). It and \(T\) satisfy \(S + T = 1\).

items.title: Second-order response
items.text: Symbol Means Also written \(\zeta\) Damping ratio. Universal; no competing symbol. \(\omega_\mathrm{n}\) Natural frequency, rad/s. \(\omega_0\) and \(w_\mathrm{n}\) are both common, and you may well have seen either. \(\omega_\mathrm{d}\) Damped frequency, \(\omega_\mathrm{d} = \omega_\mathrm{n}\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}\) — the frequency a decaying oscillation actually runs at. Informally ringing, though more in electrical and signal work than for mechanical systems. \(\zeta'\), \(\omega_\mathrm{n}'\), \(\omega_\mathrm{d}'\) The same three for the closed loop, as against the plant's own. A prime always means "after the loop is closed": on a proportional loop, \(\omega_\mathrm{n}'\) rises with gain and \(\zeta'\) falls, while the plant's \(\zeta\) and \(\omega_\mathrm{n}\) sit exactly where they were. Subscript cl, \(\zeta_\mathrm{cl}\), in some books. \(M_\mathrm{p}\) Overshoot: how far the step response goes past its final value, as a percentage of it. P.O., and percent overshoot written out. Beware: some books use \(M_\mathrm{p}\) for the resonant peak of a frequency response instead, which is a different quantity — context decides. \(t_\mathrm{r}\) Rise time. \(T_\mathrm{r}\). \(t_\mathrm{p}\) Peak time. \(T_\mathrm{p}\). \(t_\mathrm{s}\) Settling time, to a 2% band unless said otherwise. \(T_\mathrm{s}\), which also means sample time — we use \(t_\mathrm{s}\) to keep them apart. \(e_\mathrm{ss}\) Steady-state error. \(e(\infty)\). \(y_\mathrm{ss}\) Steady-state output. \(y(\infty)\).

items.title: Controllers
items.text:
Symbol Means Also written \(K_\mathrm{p}\) Proportional gain. \(K_P\) uppercase in Dorf and in many courses. Same thing. \(K_\mathrm{i}\) Integral gain. \(K_I\). \(K_\mathrm{d}\) Derivative gain. \(K_D\). \(T_\mathrm{i}\) Integral time, \(T_\mathrm{i} = K_\mathrm{p}/K_\mathrm{i}\). Used in the standard form of PID, below. \(T_\mathrm{d}\) Derivative time, \(T_\mathrm{d} = K_\mathrm{d}/K_\mathrm{p}\). \(N\) Derivative filter ratio. We use \(N = 10\) throughout. \(1/T_\mathrm{f}\) forms appear too. \(K_\mathrm{u}\) Ultimate gain, in Ziegler–Nichols tuning. \(K_\mathrm{cr}\), critical gain.

Parallel form, which is what we use and what MATLAB's pid object takes:

\[ C(s) = K_\mathrm{p} + \frac{K_\mathrm{i}}{s} + K_\mathrm{d}s. \]

Standard form, which you will meet in industry and in Dorf:

\[ C(s) = K_\mathrm{p}\left(1 + \frac{1}{T_\mathrm{i}s} + T_\mathrm{d}s\right). \]

Same controller, different parameters, and converting between them is a skill the unit will ask for.

items.title: Frequency domain
items.text: Symbol Means Also written \(\omega\) Frequency, rad/s unless stated. \(f\) in Hz; \(\omega = 2\pi f\). \(\lvert G(j\omega)\rvert\) Magnitude — the vertical axis of a Bode plot, in decibels. Very often called gain, and written "Gain (dB)". We say magnitude, because gain is already doing three other jobs: loop gain, DC gain and gain margin. MATLAB and Dorf both label the axis Magnitude. \(\angle G(j\omega)\) Phase, in degrees. \(\arg G(j\omega)\), \(\phi\), \(\Phi\). dB Decibels, \(20\log_{10}\lvert G\rvert\) for a gain. The \(10\log_{10}\) form is for power; we never use it. \(\omega_\mathrm{c}\) Corner, or break, frequency of a first-order factor: \(\omega_\mathrm{c} = 1/\tau\). \(\omega_\mathrm{b}\), and cut-off frequency, which is the commoner name in signals and filtering. \(\omega_\mathrm{gc}\) Gain crossover: where \(\lvert L \rvert = 1\), i.e. 0 dB. \(\omega_\mathrm{c}\) in some books, which is why we keep \(\omega_\mathrm{c}\) for the corner. \(\omega_\mathrm{pc}\) Phase crossover: where \(\angle L = -180^\circ\). \(\omega_{180}\). GM Gain margin — how much the loop gain can rise before instability. \(G_\mathrm{m}\), \(K_\mathrm{g}\). PM Phase margin, in degrees. \(P_\mathrm{m}\), \(\phi_\mathrm{m}\), \(\gamma\).

items.title: Laplace and the s-plane
items.text:
Symbol Means Also written \(s = \sigma + j\omega\) The Laplace variable. \(j\) \(\sqrt{-1}\). \(i\) in mathematics and physics. Engineering uses \(j\) because \(i\) is current. \(X(s)\) Laplace transform of \(x(t)\). Capital for the transform, lower case for the signal. \(\mathcal{L}\{x(t)\}\). \(\dot y\), \(\ddot y\) First and second derivatives with respect to time. \(\dot y = \mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t\). \(\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t\) and \(\mathrm{d}^2y/\mathrm{d}t^2\), which you will see at least as often. The dot is Newton's; the fraction is Leibniz's. Both are used here, the dot where an equation would otherwise get crowded. A dot always means a time derivative, never anything else. \(\sigma\) Real part of a pole — sets how fast a response decays.

Found something we use that isn't here, or a name for it we've missed? Tell me — either way it's a gap worth closing.

The unit's complete reading list is here, also linked from Blackboard, and it has a good deal more on it: alternative textbooks, the flight-dynamics half's reading, and the video series below. Editions and availability change there during the year and not here, so treat it as the current version.

Two of the video series on it are worth calling out, because for a lot of people they work better than any book:

  • Brian Douglas, Control System Lectures, at engineeringmedia.com. Short, unhurried videos that build intuition before algebra. If a Bode plot or a root locus has never quite made sense as a picture, start here. He also makes the MATLAB Tech Talks, which cover much of this unit.
  • Steve Brunton, Control Bootcamp, a playlist on YouTube. A full course, pitched a little higher, and unusually good on state space and on why the frequency domain and the time domain are two views of one thing.

items.title: A free second opinion
items.text:
If Dorf and Bishop doesn't suit you, a different author's explanation of the same idea is often exactly what's needed, and one good one costs nothing:

Åström, K. J. and Murray, R. M. (2021). Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers, 2nd edition. Princeton University Press. The authors' page at Caltech, and the book itself as one PDF (33 MB).

The whole book is on that site as a PDF, chapter by chapter or in one file, put there by the authors. It is worth reading for two things in particular:

  • Sensitivity, robustness and the limits of what feedback can do. This is the book's strongest material, and it goes further than Dorf.
  • A different route through the subject. It reaches state space early and the frequency domain late, the opposite way round from this unit. That makes it a genuine second opinion rather than a paraphrase: if an idea hasn't landed one way round, try the other.

It is pitched at scientists as well as engineers, so it is more mathematical and less aircraft-shaped than Dorf. Treat it as somewhere to go when you want depth, not as a parallel text to read alongside the handouts.

It's free, but it isn't open

The publisher has allowed the authors to keep the book on the web: "Copyright in this book is held by Princeton University Press, who have kindly agreed to allow us to keep the book available on the web." That is permission to host, not a Creative Commons licence, and it is not the same arrangement as this site's. Download it from the authors' own page rather than from anywhere else; don't re-post the PDF, and cite it properly if you use it in your coursework.

items.title: Lecture 1: The design cycle, end to end
items.text:
Slideshtmlpdf Code

This session runs through the whole control design cycle once, on a real physical rig. In the lecture, you will watch somebody try (and likely fail) to fly it by hand, measure what it actually does, decide what "good" means, design a controller to meet that, and then watch your own gains fly. Everything after today links to one of those steps.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • describe the control design cycle, and say where in it a given design activity sits;
  • identify a second-order model from a measured response, by reading its damping ratio, natural frequency and gain;
  • tune a PID controller in simulation to meet a stated requirement;
  • explain why a design that meets its requirement in simulation may not meet it on hardware.

Definitions

Spot the tooltips that appear when you hover or hold over the underlined terms? Use these to learn and prompt yourself. Check out the glossary and notation for more detail.

items.title: Where we are
items.text:
This unit assumes you have the mathematical fundamentals: Laplace transforms, transfer functions, poles and zeros, the standard second-order form and what \( \zeta \) and \( \omega_\mathrm{n} \) do to a response, Bode plots built from first- and second-order transfer functions, and PID in its parallel form.

The prerequisite diagnostic can help you work out what needs your attention.
path: Lecture 1: The design cycle, end to end

items.title: Design is cyclic
items.text:
There are many representations of the control system design cycle, the one we'll use here is Dorf and Bishop's, with a couple of additions.

The control system design process, based on Dorf and Bishop - additions in red.

Some things to highlight:

The specification comes before the model. If you want to be formal, steps 1 to 3 are done before anything is measured or derived. In practice, things may be messier.

Configuration is shown as a separate decision from the controller. Step 4 chooses what you are going to sense and what you are going to drive; step 6 chooses what to do with them. Picking a sensor commits you to its noise and its resolution long before any gain is chosen. These are often interdependent, hence the cycle.

The loop runs under a fixed specification. Step 7 sends you back to step 4 when the performance is unsatisfactory, but another other way out is to relax a specification in a considered way.
path: Lecture 1: The design cycle, end to end

items.title: What we'll add
items.text:
Step 8 is ours. Dorf and Bishop iterate within the design: simulate, assess, reconfigure. Hardware testing is implicit, but we're separating it out to make the sim-to-real transition clear.

You can address discrepancies in two ways. The obvious one is to update the model: go back to step 5, measure what you missed, and design again against something closer to reality.

But your model will always contain assumptions, approximations, and uncertainties - they work because the design accounts for exactly that. Later in the course we'll quantify uncertainty and robustness.
path: Lecture 1: The design cycle, end to end

items.title: Feedback is a trade-off, not a fix
items.text:
Feedback makes system behaviour different, and you choose which problems to have.

Close a feedback loop around a plant and you get:

  • disturbance rejection. A gust pushes the output, the error changes, the controller pushes back.
  • insensitivity to uncertainty or changes in the plant. The aircraft burns fuel and gets lighter; the controller deals with this.
  • the ability to adjust stability, which is the only reason the machine in the room can fly at all.

And you pay, unavoidably:

  • sensor noise. Simple feedback acts on what the sensor says, and cannot distinguish noise from signal. Whatever the sensor says, the controller will correct for.
  • the loop can go unstable, which the open plant could not do.
  • more gain brings more of both. Raising the loop gain suppresses disturbances and amplifies noise. These pull in opposite directions and no amount of cleverness makes them stop.

Hold on to the third of those. Almost every design decision in this unit is a choice about where to spend loop gain, and "turn it up" is only ever half an answer.
path: Lecture 1: The design cycle, end to end

items.title: The machine
items.text:
The laboratory rig is a Quanser 3-DOF helicopter: a beam on a pivot, two motors and rotors at one end, a counterweight at the other, with the whole assembly free to swing around a vertical column.

The rig you will fly. The beam pivots at the column, and the whole assembly turns about it.

It is a tandem-rotor helicopter, and it is worth seeing it as one before you see it as a lab rig. Quanser based the model on the Boeing HC-1B Chinook: two rotors one behind the other, the machine pitching nose-up and nose-down about its centre, and travelling around the rig.

Another way to look at it, if helicopters are not your thing: it is half a quadcopter. A quadcopter's lift is the sum of its four rotors, and it pitches and rolls by driving fore/aft or left/right pairs asymmetrically (yaw is a little more complicated).

Photographs: HC-1B Chinook prototype 61-2410, 1962, US Army, public domain; DJI Mavic 4 Pro by C.Stadler/Bwag, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The rig moves in three degrees of freedom. Quanser's axis conventions:

Axis Symbol Positive when Elevation \( \varepsilon \) the body is above horizontal; zero when level Pitch \( \rho \) the front motor is higher than the back motor ('front' per Travel direction) Travel \( \lambda \) the body rotates counter-clockwise, seen from above

Three axes, two motor inputs. You do not command elevation, pitch and travel independently: the only quantities you control are the two rotor voltages. Elevation comes from their sum, pitch from their difference, and travel is not directly commanded at all. It happens because pitch tilts the thrust sideways and the machine rotates round after it.

Before anything is switched on

The amplifier's rocker switch on the bench is the emergency stop. If the rig does something you do not like, switch the amplifier off. Know where the switch is before the motors spin.

Circled: the amplifier's power switch.

items.title: One of you is going to fly it
items.text:
Not a simulation of it, and not just one axis of it: the machine, all three degrees of freedom, on two joysticks. The claim made at the top of this session is that it cannot be flown by hand. You are about to find out whether that is true.

The task is a simple one: take off and fly for 10 seconds. It ends when you hit an axis limit. We'll vote on how long you think your classmate will last.

In the lecture, here's where things get exciting. You should definitely attend for this one.

items.title: Simplifying and modelling
items.text:
Three coupled axes, with one of them not directly controllable, is too much for most people, certainly without much practice, and it's quite an ask to dive into controlling automatically. So let's start by simplifying. Holding pitch and travel still, we'll command elevation alone (our Simulink model uses a separate lateral control loop, but we could just bolt them so they're static).

The elevation axis approximates to a standard second order transfer function:

\[ G(s) = \frac{\varepsilon(s)}{V(s)} = \frac{K\,\omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}} {s^{2} + 2\zeta\omega_\mathrm{n}s + \omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}} \]

with \( K \approx 3.4 \) degrees per volt, \( \omega_\mathrm{n} \approx 1.0 \) rad/s and \( \zeta \approx 0.06 \), fitted from a step response taken in the laboratory. You will fit your own numbers shortly and they will not be exactly these.

Read those three numbers and you already know what the machine does. It is stable (positive \( \zeta \)), but \( \zeta = 0.06 \) is almost no damping at all. The oscillation has a period of about six seconds (\( T = \frac{2 \pi}{\omega_\mathrm{n}}\)) and takes around a minute to die away.

Let's close a simple proportional feedback loop around it:

Proportional control of the elevation axis, assuming a perfect sensor.

We'll see in the lecture the effect that this has.

Why turning the gain up will not fix it

A sensible first instinct is more proportional gain. Close a proportional loop around this plant and the characteristic polynomial is

\[ s^{2} + 2\zeta\omega_\mathrm{n}s + \omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}(1 + KK_\mathrm{p}) \]

\( K_\mathrm{p} \) does not appear in the coefficient of \( s \). The real part of the closed-loop poles (the roots of the characteristic polynomial, i.e. where the characteristic equation = 0) is stuck at \( -\zeta\omega_\mathrm{n} \) whatever you do, so the poles slide straight up a vertical line: faster oscillation, less damping, and a settling time that does not move.

Going from \( K_\mathrm{p} = 0.5 \) to \( K_\mathrm{p} = 10 \) takes the overshoot from 89% to 97% and leaves the settling time at 65 seconds.

Refresher: where the characteristic polynomial comes from

Inspecting the system block diagram, then some algebra. Worth doing once by hand, because every closed loop in this unit is assembled the same way.

Read the block diagram. The junction subtracts, the controller multiplies, and the plant is the second-order TF \( G(s) \):

\[ e = \varepsilon_\mathrm{ref} - \varepsilon, \qquad V = K_\mathrm{p}e, \qquad \varepsilon = G(s)\,V \]

Substitute inwards until only \( \varepsilon \) and \( \varepsilon_\mathrm{ref} \) are left:

\[ \varepsilon = G K_\mathrm{p}\left(\varepsilon_\mathrm{ref} - \varepsilon\right) \]

Collect the \( \varepsilon \) terms on one side:

\[ \varepsilon\left(1 + K_\mathrm{p}G\right) = K_\mathrm{p}G\,\varepsilon_\mathrm{ref} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_\mathrm{ref}} = \frac{K_\mathrm{p}G}{1 + K_\mathrm{p}G} \]

That fraction is the closed-loop transfer function, and it is worth recognising on sight: forward path over one plus the loop. It is the same shape whatever sits in the two blocks.

Put the plant in. With \( G = K\omega_\mathrm{n}^{2} / \left(s^{2} + 2\zeta\omega_\mathrm{n}s + \omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}\right) \), multiply top and bottom by that denominator so the fraction inside the fraction disappears:

\[ \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_\mathrm{ref}} = \frac{K_\mathrm{p}K\omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}} {s^{2} + 2\zeta\omega_\mathrm{n}s + \omega_\mathrm{n}^{2} + K_\mathrm{p}K\omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}} = \frac{K_\mathrm{p}K\omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}} {s^{2} + 2\zeta\omega_\mathrm{n}s + \omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}\left(1 + KK_\mathrm{p}\right)} \]

The denominator is the characteristic polynomial, and setting it to zero is the characteristic equation. Everything about how this loop behaves on its own is in there; the numerator only scales what comes out.

\[ s^{2} + 2\zeta\omega_\mathrm{n}s + \omega_\mathrm{n}^{2}\left(1 + KK_\mathrm{p}\right) = 0 \]

Compare it with the standard second-order form \( s^{2} + 2\zeta'\omega_\mathrm{n}'s + \omega_\mathrm{n}'^{2} \), where the primes mark the closed loop: the plant's own \( \zeta \) and \( \omega_\mathrm{n} \) are untouched, and tuning will not touch them. The constant term gives \( \omega_\mathrm{n}' \), after which the \( s \) term gives \( \zeta' \). Look at which of the two coefficients \( K_\mathrm{p} \) appears in before you do it.

Proportional gain alone moves the poles straight up. The overshoot gets worse, the settling time does not improve, and none of them reaches the demand.

Move the gain yourself and watch which numbers follow it and which do not.

Damping ratio and natural frequency both move with the gain, by the same factor and in opposite directions. The three values marked • are the ones that do not move at all.

Worth doing deliberately: take the gain from 0 to 10 and watch \( \zeta' \) fall from 0.060 to 0.010 while \( \omega_\mathrm{n}' \) rises from 1.0 to 5.9 rad/s (the 'prime' ticks (\('\)) denote the closed-loop values). Their product is 0.060 at both ends, and at every gain in between. That product is the real part of the poles, it is the rate the envelope decays at, and it is the reason the settling time reads 65 seconds wherever you put the slider.

Damping has to come from somewhere other than \( K_\mathrm{p} \), which is only focused 'on the present': we need a derivative term, which 'looks into the future' and reduces overshoot; the steady-state error between where it settles and what you asked for needs something with memory: that is the integral term, which 'looks into the past'.

So: what would 'fixed' look like?

items.title: A requirement is a design input
items.text:
"Make it fly well" is not a clear requirement. You or a pilot could make subjective comments, and these can get you a long way, but vibes cannot be clearly met, missed, argued about, or worked with analytically, which means they cannot be designed to in the way that we want.

A validatable requirement is a number with a test attached (we'll look at more complex ones later). For a step change in commanded elevation, the ones that matter today are:

Quantity Means Typical form Overshoot, \( M_\mathrm{p} \) How far past the target it goes, as a percentage "no more than 20%" Settling time, \( t_\mathrm{s} \) Until it stays within a band of the final value "within 2% in less than 8 s" Steady-state error What is left when it stops moving "less than 1 degree"

Settling time

Always say which band a settling time refers to. We use 2% throughout, which is what MATLAB's stepinfo and Dorf both default to.

We will agree today's requirement in the room, out loud, before anybody designs anything.

You have a target. You still need a model to design against.
path: Lecture 1: The design cycle, end to end

items.title: Identifying the plant from what it actually does
items.text:
You could compute \( K \) from the geometry and physics (see the Flight Dynamics part of the unit). We will measure it instead, because the real world, real fabrication, and real wear and tear, change the properties and the behaviour.

We're going to characterise this rig using a system identification approach. The lab resources include some sample data that they use if you don't have your own measurements to-hand (we may upload the readings we take in the lecture too).

Once we've uploaded our in-lecture data and you've downloaded it, open identify_rig.m from the laboratory folder. It walks you through fitting the rig by hand, then automatically, and saves your model down where everything else can read it.

Download the laboratory folder

Core expectation: generate a manual second-order fit from a measured response:

  • the period of the oscillation gives the damped frequency, \( \omega_\mathrm{d} = 2\pi / T_\mathrm{d} \);
  • the ratio of successive peaks gives the damping ratio, by log decrement;
  • the steady state value gives the gain.

Going further: tfest will fit a model of whatever order you ask for in one line. Do the fit by hand first to get a feel for the process and the system, and check the tfest docs to understand how it works.

Variability in models

You will not all get the same numbers from the same response. Where you read the peaks, how much of the tail you trust: all of it affects the answer. Comparing fits and getting a 'feel' for what is 'sensible' is part of the exercise.

items.title: Tuning, and then flying
items.text:
To do in the lab

2026: We didn't get to this section in the lecture because I talk too much. Make sure you work through the lab parts 1-3, these will get you familiar with tuning a PID controller on the Quansers.

Continue through the lab resources - in simulation, you tune a PID controller until it meets the requirement you agreed, then submit your gains to me. s2_tune checks them and hands you a link with your numbers already filled in (only do this in the lecture - you don't need to submit lab values); you press Submit yourself, so you see exactly what goes out under your name.

The files are yours, and the recording comes with them, so none of this depends on being in the room when it happens. If you did not get through it in the session, or you want to try a second design, run the session code yourself and submit from there.

The check simulates what the rig does, which is not quite what step does: the demand is ramped rather than stepped, and the derivative acts on the measured angle rather than on the error. Expect its numbers to differ from your own plot by a little. The hardware will differ by more, and that gap is the last section of this handout.

We'll fly three rounds:

  1. The extremes, chosen because they misbehave: the most aggressive, the most sluggish, the most integral. Cause and effect before any good answer.
  2. The cohort average. Often worse than most of its parts, which is worth watching: the average of safe designs is not safe by construction.
  3. The best few.

Every submission is checked before it reaches the hardware, against the model fitted from the rig on the day, and gains outside the envelope are refused rather than adjusted. Not against your own fit: your fit is an estimate of the machine, and my real machine has to survive the flight. If yours are refused you will be told which limit they missed.

Your name, on screen, in front of everybody

The form asks for a display name, and that is the name on screen when your gains fly. Choose an alias if you would rather. Your University account is recorded by the form so that I know whose submission is whose, but it is never shown to the room.

items.title: Where simulation and hardware disagree
items.text:
Your design will meet the requirement in simulation. Some of them will not meet it on the rig. The gap is not carelessness; it's one of our core learning outcomes.

Four reasons it happens, all of which get a week of their own later:

  • The model is wrong a simplification. It is a linearisation of one axis of a machine that has three, fitted from one response over a few seconds.
  • The actuators have limits. The motors saturate. A controller that demands 30 V from a 24 V amplifier won't get what it wants.
  • There is noise. The encoder quantises (steps in discrete increments), and derivative action amplifies exactly that.
  • The plant moves. Trim shifts, friction changes, and nothing about the rig at 14:00 is quite what it was at 13:00.

The cycle's answer is not to build a better model before designing. It is to design, test, find out where you were wrong, go round again, and account for uncertainty in your design.

That is one full design cycle. In future lectures we'll look at each step in detail.
path: Lecture 1: The design cycle, end to end

items.title: Summary
items.text:
• Control design is a loop: understand, specify, design, simulate, test, repeat. Every week of this unit is one step of it.
  • Feedback is a tradeoff. It gives you disturbance rejection, insensitivity and stabilisation, and it costs you noise on the output and the possibility of instability. More gain brings more of both.
  • A requirement is a design input: a number with a test, agreed before the design, not after.
  • A model you measured beats a model you assumed (although there is utility in modelling from the fundamentals), and knowing which one you have is important.
  • Simulation and hardware often disagree, we can design for this.

How the unit runs

The schedule, the assessment, the laboratory and what a week looks like are on Introduction and logistics.

items.title: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust
items.text:
Slideshtmlpdf Code

There is no right answer until you say what you want. In this session you will write requirements that can be met, missed or argued about, and you will learn what you need to know about a model to understand its utility..

Learning outcomes

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • write measurable time- and frequency-domain requirements, and justify each from a vehicle's role or handling qualities;
  • validate a linear model against measured or flight-test data, quantifying where it fits and where it does not;
  • explain linearisation about a trim condition, and identify when a design leaves the region where it holds;
  • state the assumptions a model rests on, and bound its uncertainty for use in design.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: Where we are
items.text:
You have fitted a second-order model to a measured response, agreed a requirement out loud, and designed a controller against that model. Three questions before any of today's material, and answer them before you read on:

  1. You fitted \( K \), \( \omega_\mathrm{n} \) and \( \zeta \) from one recording. Which of the three do you trust most, and which least?
  2. A classmate's fit differs from yours by 10% in \( \zeta \). Is one of you wrong?
  3. Your design met the requirement in simulation. What would have to be true for it to meet the requirement on the rig?
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: How much of a problem is this?
items.text:
Here is the model, simulated with the step that was actually applied, drawn on top of the recording it was fitted to. Note the residual - more on that later.

The fitted model against the recording it came from. The first ten seconds are shaded: that is the window the model's starting state was matched over.

Before you read the next paragraph, commit to an answer. The model and the machine disagree. How much of a problem is this?

It depends entirely on what you are going to do with the model, and that is the first idea of the session. Over the first 10 s the two traces differ by 2.8% of the 6.80 degrees the step asked for, with a worst case of 0.41 degrees. Over the first 60 s they differ by 8.9%, worst case 1.33 degrees. The model's not bad, it's just a representation over a particular window. Whether it applies depends on what we're using it for.

This data has a defect

The arm was already swinging through 4.21 degrees when the step arrived. M.003 is a busy room: four of these rigs close together, a bank of TQ modular air-flow benches, and the ventilation, which is the biggest single source of disturbance. A step response starts from rest, so a model simulated from rest begins in the wrong place.

L02_validate.m fits the starting state along with the rest, over the window shaded above: that is how the model and the machine were put in the same place, and MATLAB's own compare does the same thing. Retaking it would have been better, which is why Part 1 of the laboratory asks you to plot every trace before you leave the room and take it again if the arm is still moving.

A steady start still only gives you one model, fitted at one trim elevation and one step size. How widely it applies is a good question, and no single recording answers it. Taking the same step from a different trim, and different step sizes from the same trim, gives you more of an idea about that.

So: what would a requirement have to say for this argument to be settleable?
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: A requirement is a number, a test, and a reason
items.text:
You already have the first two. A requirement names a quantity, gives it a number, and says how you would measure it: "settles within 2% of the demand inside 8 seconds, measured from a 7.5 degree step". The third is what separates a requirement from a preference.

Every number in a requirement comes from somewhere, and you have to be able to say where. Here are four possible sources:

Where the number came from Example The vehicle's job A surveying aircraft holds a line to a tolerance set by the camera's swath. A published handling-qualities criterion A closed-loop damping ratio inside the band the applicable standard allows for that class of aircraft and that phase of flight. A physical limit you measured The demand saturates 8.6 V above the trim, so the controller may ask for no more than 6.0 V. An agreement in the room "Eight seconds", because nobody could think of a reason for six or ten.

The last one is legitimate. What is not legitimate is dressing it up as one of the first three. Write "agreed, no stronger basis" beside it and revisit it when there is one.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: What a requirement asks of your model
items.text:
A time-domain requirement is also a statement about frequency, whether or not it is written that way. For a response dominated by a second-order pair, overshoot fixes the damping ratio and the settling time then fixes the natural frequency:

\[ \zeta = \frac{-\ln M_\mathrm{p}}{\sqrt{\pi^{2} + \ln^{2} M_\mathrm{p}}}, \qquad \omega_\mathrm{n} = \frac{4}{\zeta\,t_\mathrm{s}} \]

with \( M_\mathrm{p} \) the overshoot as a fraction and \( t_\mathrm{s} \) the settling time to 2%. So:

Requirement \( \zeta \) \( \omega_\mathrm{n} \) Settle to 2% in 1.5 s, overshoot at most 10% 0.591 4.51 rad/s Settle to 2% in 2.0 s, overshoot at most 10% 0.591 3.38 rad/s Settle to 2% in 3.0 s, overshoot at most 10% 0.591 2.26 rad/s Settle to 2% in 4.0 s, overshoot at most 20% 0.456 2.19 rad/s

That \( \omega_\mathrm{n} \) is the frequency the closed loop will be working at. Your model has to be right there. A requirement asking for 4.51 rad/s on a model validated at 2 rad/s will cause you problems, however carefully the simulation was run.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: Make these testable
items.text:
Here are some things you (or a less-enlightened control designer) might say. Rewrite each one as a requirement, and against each one name which of the four sources its number came from.

  1. "It should feel crisp."
  2. "It mustn't wander off while the camera is running."
  3. "Don't let it fight the pilot."

For each, write down one number you had to invent and what you would do to find the right value.

Core expectation: a quantity, a number and a test for at least one of the three.

Going further: all three, with its source named for each, and an argument about the third, which is the only one of them with a person in the loop.

Compare with the pair next to you: you might not agree, which makes for some good learning.

You have a requirement. Now, what does it take to use it to design against a model?
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: What makes a model trustworthy
items.text:
Not being right. Nothing is right. A model is trustworthy when we know three things:

  • Over what range of frequency, or over what time. The elevation model above holds for 10 s and not for 60 s.
  • Over what amplitude, and about what trim. Every linearisation is taken about an operating point, and the model is a claim about motion near it.
  • How far out it is inside that range. A number, from a residual.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: Read the residual, not the fit percentage
items.text:
A fit percentage hides a great deal

Two traps, both common.

MATLAB likes to give you a 'fit percentage', but doesn't tell you much about what it actually is. RMSE (root-mean-squared error) is useful but obscures a lot.

Fitted over what? Match the elevation model's starting state over the whole 60 s instead of the first 10 s. The 60 s residual improves a little, from 8.9% to 8.3%, and the 10 s residual more than doubles, from 2.8% to 6.7%. Least squares spreads the error over whatever you hand it, so you have traded accuracy where the model was good for accuracy where it was never going to be. The window is part of the answer and has to be quoted with it.

Against what? A residual of 5% is unreadable until you say 5% of what. Throughout this session it is a percentage of the change the model says the input will produce, which is a number you have before you measure anything and which is comparable between recordings of different size. A percentage of the signal's own range is neither.

Subtract the model's response from the measurement and you get the residual. Its size is one piece of information and its shape can tell you even more:

What the residual looks like What it is telling you Flat, and the size of the sensor noise Nothing systematic left. The model is as good as the measurement. A slow drift one way Lots of potential causes. Maybe the trim shifted? An oscillation at the signal's own frequency, growing (and then maybe shrinking) with time The frequency is out. The two start together and separate by a little each cycle. An oscillation at some other frequency The plant has a mode that this model does not represent.

The last two are the useful ones, and neither is particularly evident in a single fit percentage. The earlier figure shows the third case: the residual is small for two oscillations, then grows into a wave at the same frequency as the signal. A small error in \( \omega_\mathrm{n} \) accumulates as phase, and after enough cycles the model's peaks arrive where the measurement's troughs are.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: Linearisation holds near the trim, and "near" is a number
items.text:
A linear model comes from a nonlinear machine by taking the first term of a Taylor expansion about an operating point. That is exact at the operating point and approximate away from it, and the question a design has to answer is: how far away is still close enough?

The answer is never just "small". Small compared with what? The honest version names a quantity and a number, and the only way to get one is to excite the machine at two sizes and compare. You will do exactly that twice today, on two different (simulated) machines, and get a different answer each time.

Four assumptions sit behind the elevation model you fitted, and each one names a way it can fail:

The model assumes Where that gives way The arm swings about a fixed trim elevation. Gravity's restoring moment on an arm goes as \( \sin\varepsilon \), so the stiffness, and with it \( \omega_\mathrm{n} \), depends on the trim you fly about. The swing about that trim is small. A larger swing covers more of that curve, so the frequency you fit moves with the amplitude you fit it at. Friction is viscous, proportional to rate. Anything dry or sticking takes a different fraction out of a small swing than a large one. Elevation moves on its own. The three axes are coupled, and this model only has one input and one output.

The first two are settled by measurement rather than by argument, which is what Part 1 of the laboratory is asking for when it suggests repeating the step from a different trim and at a different size. Two recordings answer a question one cannot. (We can also infer from a physics-based model, but who has time for that?)

What a linear model cannot do, whatever its coefficients:

  • change its gain with the size of the input. Double the input and the output doubles, exactly.
  • change its natural frequency with the size of the motion. One set of poles, one frequency, every amplitude.

So any measured dependence on amplitude is outside the model by construction, and no amount of refitting brings it inside.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: Where the rig's model fits, and where it doesn't
items.text:
Open L02_validate.m and run it on your own recording, or on the sample if you have not got one of your own. It starts the model where the arm actually was, draws the residual, and then measures the period of the oscillation one cycle at a time.

Download the Lecture 2 folder

Core expectation: the overlay and the residual table, 2.8% over the first 10 s against 8.9% over 60 s, and a residual whose shape you can name. Drag the fit window and watch both numbers move.

Going further: what the period does as the swing decays, cycle by cycle. Predict which way it goes before you look.

The script pairs each recording with the model that was fitted to it: your own fit against your own recording, and the shipped model against the shipped sample. There are four rigs in the laboratory and they do not share a model, so crossing the two would make the residual a comparison between two machines rather than a statement about either.

Then look at what the period does as the swing decays.

Five cycles of the same recording. The period falls as the swing decays, so the natural frequency you fit depends on the amplitude you fit it at. Times indicate start time of that oscillation in the measured data.

The period falls from 6.213 s when the arm is swinging through 6.03 degrees to 5.967 s when it is swinging through 1.19 degrees, about 4%. Below a swing of about ten encoder counts, which on this rig is 0.086 degrees each, the peaks are likely disturbances rather than the rig, so the measurement stops there.

Before believing it, check it against something that cannot fail the same way. Those five periods are gaps between crossings of the final value, so they are only as good as the final value you assumed:

Cycle begins at Period Swing about the final value 1.89 s 6.213 s 6.03° 8.10 s 6.098 s 4.22° 14.20 s 6.069 s 2.93° 20.27 s 5.933 s 1.73° 26.20 s 5.967 s 1.19°

The script also times peak to peak and trough to trough, neither of which uses the final value at all. Both fall the same way. Their individual figures move by a few hundredths of a second between runs and between implementations, because the peak of a signal quantised to 0.086° has a flat top and the exact sample you call the peak is a choice. The trend survives all of it; the third decimal place does not, so do not quote it.

Why does it do that?

Something about this machine depends on how far it is moving. Which something is an open question in this laboratory: the obvious candidates are the way the restoring moment varies with elevation, and friction. Are there experiments we could do to identify this?

You do not need the cause to act on the measurement. A linear model has one natural frequency and this machine does not, so the fit is a claim about one amplitude, whatever the reason. Be clear about this when you describe and share your models.

Agree with your neighbour on one sentence: the elevation model may be used for …. Keep it, because it is the shape of what you write in the second hour.

Now the same job on something you did not fit yourself.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: The case: a pitch model and two flight-test records
items.text:
A small fixed-wing aircraft. The flight dynamics side of the house has derived a third-order pitch model from its geometry and its aerodynamic data and handed it over:

\[ G(s) = \frac{\theta(s)}{\delta_\mathrm{e}(s)} = \frac{40}{s\,(s+2)\,(s+10)} \]

in degrees of attitude per degree of elevator. Pitch rate lags the elevator with a time constant of 0.5 s and a steady gain of 2 (deg/s) per degree, the servo lags by 0.1 s, and attitude is the integral of pitch rate.

You have also been handed two flight-test records, 60 s each, logged at 50 Hz, with elevator, pitch rate and pitch attitude. Both fly the same test card:

  • a 3-2-1-1: four held elevator segments of 3, 2, 1 and 1 seconds, alternating in sign. It puts energy over about a decade of frequency around the fast pitching motion.
  • then a pulse held for three seconds and released, which is how a slow mode is excited.

One record flies the card at 2 degrees of elevator input, the other at 8 degrees. (NB: a 'test card' is the instruction sheet that a pilot uses to fly a defined set of activities, of which a '3-2-1-1' is a classic. An example is in the video below; note that this is roll and yaw not elevator).

These records are synthetic

They were generated by a model, no aircraft was flown. The structure of what you will find is real: all of it happens to real models against real flight test, and the reasons are the same.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: Validate it, bound it, write the requirement
items.text:
Open L02_uav_case.m, with uav-doublets.mat beside it. You'll either need them in the lab folder, to add both folders to your MATLAB workspace.

Download the Lecture 2 folder

Core expectation, plot the overlaid test data and model response, and their residual, then review the three findings below.

Going further: write the bound the model may be used inside, and check one of the requirements you wrote earlier against it.

Simulate the handed-over model with the elevator that was actually flown, subtract, and look at the residual in two windows.

The 2 degree record. After the elevator is released the experimental pitch rate oscillates but the model's decays to zero.

Quote the residual against the pitch rate the model says the input will produce, which is its steady gain of 2.000 (deg/s)/deg times the elevator, so 4.00 deg/s on the 2 degree record. Normalise by the aircraft's own gain instead and you are dividing by the thing you are trying to find out.

On the 2 degree record the residual is 14.2% over the 3-2-1-1 and 4.5% after the release, peaking at 0.38 deg/s. The rate gyro contributes about 0.04 deg/s RMSE, which is 1.0%, so neither number is noise.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: Observation 1: What is left after the release has a frequency
items.text:
From 24 seconds the elevator is back at zero and the model's pitch rate decays to zero with it. The record does not: it holds a smooth oscillation of period 17.9 s, which is 0.35 rad/s, and amplitude about 0.28 deg/s.

You have met that motion in the flight dynamics half of this unit. The handed-over model cannot produce it: two real poles and an integrator, so it has no oscillation available at any frequency. A residual with a frequency in it is a mode the model does not have.
path: Lecture 2: Requirements and models you can trust

items.title: Observation 2: During the fast input, the model is wrong above a frequency
items.text:
The larger residual over the 3-2-1-1 is not a missing mode, it is the model's shape. Throw away everything above a cut-off, compare what is left, and the error sorts itself by frequency:

Everything below Residual, 2 degree record Residual, 8 degree record 0.5 rad/s 1.0% 1.8% 1.0 rad/s 1.8% 2.8% 1.5 rad/s 3.2% 3.6% 2.0 rad/s 5.1% 4.6% 3.0 rad/s 8.5% 7.1% 5.0 rad/s 12.0% 10.2% 10 rad/s 13.8% 12.0%

The model is not wrong. It is wrong above about 2 rad/s, and that is a sentence a designer can act on. The two records agree on where the error lives and disagree about how much of it there is, which the next section explains.

The aircraft the records came from, beside the handed-over model. The shaded band is where they agree to within 2 dB and 15 degrees: 0.37 to 2.35 rad/s, about four fifths of a decade.

The figure compares the frequency-domain response of the model with the experimental response of the aircraft. Compare the band it marks, 0.37 to 2.35 rad/s, with the cut-off table you built from the data alone. The lower edge is the slow mode and the upper edge is where things diverge at higher frequencies. Note we've defined our range of validity - 'within 2dB and 15 degrees'.
